newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil cautiously upbeat on Real Plan anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Brazil cautiously upbeat on Real Plan anniversary.

text.p: As Brazil approaches the third anniversary of its inflation-fighting Real Plan, the package enjoys the support of a majority of citizens but could still fall foul of a series of looming problems, newspapers said.

Most residents of Sao Paulo believe the Real Plan -- which turns three on Tuesday -- is a success and has benefited the poor, according to a poll commissioned by daily newspaper O Estado de Sao Paulo.

Some 71 percent are totally or partially in favor of the measures, up from 66 percent a year ago, while 57 percent believe the plan has helped the poor, up from 37 percent in 1996, the survey by InformEstado showed.

The main reason behind the renewed wave of optimism was economic growth with low inflation and an increase in consumer credit, which has allowed many to improve their standard of living, the newspaper said.
In Rio de Janeiro state, 61.5 percent of respondents gave a thumbs-up to the Real Plan, up from 52 percent in September last year, according to a poll conducted by Jornal do Brasil/Gerp.
But more than half were worried about unemployment and the plan's popularity fell among middle-class and higher-income families, who said they had benefited less than the poor.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, in an editorial published by Folha de Sao Paulo, said Brazil was entering a new cycle of prosperity and the plan was reducing the drastic income inequalities which have long plagued the country.

"In these three years of the Real Plan, what gratifies me most is knowing that 13 million Brazilians stepped over the poverty line, are eating better and buying consumer goods which make life less hard," Cardoso wrote.
"No other economic plan in the world has incorporated so many people in so little time," he said. "This time, the cake is not only growing but it is better divided."
Now, Brazil must accelerate the pace of economic and social reforms and tackle the problem of its growing trade deficit and dependency on foreign financing, newspapers said.

"If nowadays we are still not growing like 'tigers', it is only a function of the resistance to reforms," Central Bank international affairs director Gustavo Franco wrote in an article published by O Estado de Sao Paulo.

Finance Minister Pedro Malan, in a variety of interviews published on Sunday, said that without reforms the public sector would become unviable but added that Brazil's burgeoning trade deficit was sustainable, for now.
"We don't see any difficulty in the next two years for financing this deficit," Malan told O Estado.

"I would be preoccupied if this was being done with volatile capital as has happened in other countries. But 42.5 percent of the current account deficit is being financed by direct investment," he added.

Inflation was likely to fall below this year's forecast seven percent in 1998, Malan told O Globo newspaper, although he declined to give a more specific figure. "We will have an (inflation) rate of less than the seven percent we expect this year," Malan said. "But some things still need to be done to consolidate the relative stability of the currency's purchasing power."
Meanwhile, consumption was growing too fast in some sectors although the government does not yet plan any measures to limit spending. "Car sales are preoccupying," Malan told O Estado.
In the face of these problems, Brazil's privatization program will remain a key pillar to the continued success of the Real Plan, according to a study published in O Estado.

Brazil stands to earn a potential $80 billion between the second half of 1997 and the year 2000 from the sale of public companies, the study by Citibank shows. Of this, $30 billion will come from foreign participation, it said.
"Privatizations will, without a doubt, help the government finance its external deficit," Citibank economist Felipe Macedo de Holanda told the newspaper.
